extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; aspiring essayists and writers of satirical/social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing short satirical/social essays that blend moral reflection, anecdote, classical learning, and observational humor as exemplified in The Spectator. Focuses on devices, tones, and structural choices used to expose manners and entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physiognomy/physical observation to sketch character
rubrics_metrics.description: Every one is in some Degree a Master of that Art which is generally distinguished by the Name of Physiognomy; and naturally forms to himself the Character or Fortune of a Stranger, from the Features and Lineaments of his Face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ close observation of faces and outward appearance (the air of the whole face, not merely lines) to suggest humour, temper, or social role. Use physical detail to create immediate character impressions, but balance this with caution about prejudice: 'a wise Man should be particularly cautious how he gives credit to a Man's outward Appearance.' Illustrate with anecdotes (e.g., Socrates and the physiognomist) showing both the power and the danger of judgments from looks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against simple prejudgment from looks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an irreparable Injustice we are guilty of towards one another, when we are prejudiced by the Looks and Features of those whom we do not know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While physical traits are useful comic material, avoid endorsing crude determinism. Use examples showing virtue contradicting appearance (e.g., 'There is a double Praise due to Virtue, when it is lodged in a Body that seems to have been prepared for the Reception of Vice') to teach readers not to mistake surface for substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame essays around letters from correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the comic situations and complaints are presented as Letters of my Correspondents... (e.g., letters from ROSALINDA, T.T., Philo-Britannicus, Sam Hopewell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fictional or real-sounding letters to introduce diverse voices, local colour, and anecdotal evidence. Letters let you present multiple perspectives, comic specifics, and punchy details (P.S. notes, dates, signatures) and provide a natural prompt for your response or moralizing commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin type-names to satirize social kinds (labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall distinguish this Sect of Women by the Title of 'Demurrers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create concise, memorable labels for recurring foolish or fashionable types (coquettes, 'Idols', 'Demurrers', etc.). Such naming condenses critique into an easily recognized comic archetype and gives you a recurring target for jokes and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend moral reflection with amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: All that I intend, is, to advise them, when they are prompted by Reason and Inclination, to demurr only out of Form, and so far as Decency requires... A virtuous Woman should reject the first Offer of Marriage...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine humorous exposure of follies with explicit moral lessons or practical advice. After comic examples, offer reflections (e.g., on the shortness of life, decay of beauty) to give essays gravity and social purpose without killing the wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical and literary allusions for authority and flourish
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations and references to Ovid, Martial, Virgil, Plato, Milton, etc., are interspersed throughout the papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy short classical quotations, epigrams, and poetic excerpts to lend learned authority, heighten irony, or provide contrasting high-style rhetoric against low comic material. Use them judiciously as illustrative ornaments or as moral confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate abstract points with vivid anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall translate a Story... Monsieur Pontignan speaking of a Love-Adventure... gives the following Account... (the mummy/swaddling story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, sometimes absurd anecdotes dramatize the principle you're discussing (e.g., Tantalism, demurrage). Choose scenes with sensory detail and a clear comic payoff; place them after a brief generalization to make the abstract memorable and entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize manners by depicting everyday social settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of behaviour in Coffee-houses, Taverns, Hide-Park, the Theatres, and about Servants illustrate national habits and follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set scenes in familiar public places to expose fashions, affectations, and hypocrisies. The ordinary public sphere (coffee-houses, alehouses, parks) supplies ready comic material and grounds social critique in recognizable behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix serious argument with irony and understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Diffidence and Presumption, upon account of our Persons, are equally Faults... I would not however be understood... to discourage that natural Modesty...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ironic contrast (praise that reads as critique; grave-sounding admonitions about trivialities) and measured understatement to make satire bite without alienating readers. Let moral counsel peek through the humour to keep tone balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parody notices and faux-publications as satirical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: ADVERTISEMENT. This to give Notice, That the three Criticks... will meet this next Sunday... to finish the Merits of several Dramatick Writers: And will also make an End of the Nature of True Sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody the forms of public announcements, advertisements, or reviews to mock literary fashions and the pretensions of critics. Short faux-ads are crisp vehicles for satire and can punctuate an essay with a pointed gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse and translate authoritative stories for rhetorical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall translate a Story that has been quoted upon another Occasion by one of the most learned Men of the present Age...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reworking tales from learned sources or foreign anecdotes gives essays a cosmopolitan air and shows erudition; such stories can be tailored for comic magnification and to connect contemporary follies to longstanding human habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ epigrammatic lines and short verse to sharpen points
rubrics_metrics.description: Martial's epigram and passages from Virgil and Dryden are used to epitomize or dramatize observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert brief poetic quotations or epigrams as punchlines, ironic counters, or rhetorical emphasis. Use them to encapsulate a moral or to raise comedic contrast between loftiness of verse and pettiness of subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt multiple personae and signed voices for variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers alternate between Addison and Steele (signed 'R.' in one paper), and include correspondent voices with distinct tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary voice via authorial signatures, fictional correspondents, and different rhetorical stances to present a chorus of views and keep readers engaged. Distinct voices allow different kinds of humour (curmudgeonly, sentimental, ironic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neologisms and learned terms for comic authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Moore...reckons this particular Inclination... gives it the Name of a 'Prosopolepsia'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce or cite rare/learned words (real or mock-scientific) to lampoon pretension and to give humorous precision to social vices. Such coinages can become running jokes or concise labels for recurring themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the essay: present complaint, exemplify, then prescribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters present complaints (e.g., about servants, demurrers), followed by general observations, anecdotes, and concluding reflections or remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize pieces so an opening situation or letter leads to broader reflection, supported by examples and concluding with a clear takeaway or prescription. This arc turns gossip into argument and gives an entertaining moral shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use footnotes and learned asides for authority and comic annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive footnotes reference sources (Cicero, Plato, Baptista della Porta, etc.) and supply glosses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add footnotes to provide scholarly backing, witty clarifications, or ironic commentary that runs parallel to the main text. Footnotes let you be both learned and playful without interrupting narrative flow.
